subject: AI & Agents
title: The First AI Winter
description: A quick win: understand The First AI Winter.

hook.text: By 1974, AI had promised the moon and delivered a flashlight. Funders pulled the plug.

buildup.text: The Lighthill Report in the UK declared AI research had failed to deliver on its promises.

discovery.text: Government funding dried up. Labs closed. Researchers scattered to other fields.

twist.text: The technology wasn't wrong — the timeline predictions were. Decades too optimistic.

climax.text: The survivors kept working quietly, planting seeds that would bloom 20 years later.

quiz.question: What triggered the first AI winter?
options: AI failed to deliver on overly optimistic promises
A computer virus destroyed AI research
AI became too dangerous to continue

details.summary: The first AI winter in the 1970s saw funding collapse after early AI failed to deliver on its grand promises. Machines could not understand language or reason as researchers had predicted.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding AI winters helps recognize today's hype patterns. The cycle of inflated expectations followed by disappointment is recurring, and awareness is the best defense against bad investments.
takeaways: Funding collapsed in the 1970s when AI failed to deliver
Overpromising led to massive disillusionment with the field
The hype-disappointment cycle is a recurring AI pattern

faq.question: What caused the first AI winter?
faq.answer: Researchers promised human-level language understanding and reasoning within years. When progress stalled, funders including DARPA dramatically cut AI research budgets, and the field entered a period of decline.

faq.question: How long did the first AI winter last?
faq.answer: Roughly from the mid-1970s to the early 1980s, when expert systems briefly revived commercial interest. The exact boundaries are debated, but reduced funding persisted for several years.
